title: Cooking as practice
hookLine: a recipe video at double speed, and a Zen cook who treats the rice as his own eyes
tomorrow: who sleeps well on frozen ground, on a bed of leaves?

lines: DOUBLE SPEED, DONE IN A MINUTE.
RICE AND WATER AS YOUR OWN EYES.
CAN STIRRING A POT BE PRACTICE?
cards: Recipe videos run at double speed: a blur of hands, a sizzle, done in a minute. Real cooking is slower, and often it feels like a chore between you and the meal.
The Zen teacher Dogen wrote a whole set of instructions for the monastery cook, and he didn't treat the kitchen as a chore at all.
He wrote that the cook should look after the rice and the water as if they were his own eyes. So here's the question for today: can stirring a pot be practice?

teach.h: OTHERS ARE NOT ME. IF NOT NOW, WHEN?
teach.b: Dogen's answer is yes, and he tells a story to prove it. As a young monk in China, he met an old temple cook drying mushrooms under a hot sun, sweating, with no hat. Dogen asked why he didn't let a helper do it.
The cook said: others are not me. Then why in this heat? If not now, when?
Dogen wrote that he understood the cook's work only then.

The cook isn't waiting to get back to practice. Washing rice, picking out grit, watching the flame: that is the practice, done with the care you'd give your own eyes. Now a neighbor who says something close.
In a Christian monastery, a kitchen brother named Lawrence said that the time of work was no different for him from the time of prayer; he could turn a little omelet in the pan for the love of God.
And the King James Bible has Paul's line: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
Shared: the pot and the flame aren't a break from the holy life, and full-hearted attention belongs in the kitchen.
Different, and honestly so: Brother Lawrence and Paul turn the work toward God.
Dogen's cook turns his whole attention to the rice itself, and the attention is the practice.

how: In Zen monasteries the head cook (tenzo) holds a respected post, and kitchen work is treated as practice; some lay Buddhists cook in silence or bow to the stove before beginning.

o: a vegetarian diet required of every Buddhist
cooking done with full care, as practice itself
cooking food to offer only on festival days

games.q: the cook's story — tap the pairs.
p: wrote instructions for the temple cook
dried mushrooms in the hot sun
why he didn't hand the job off

s: in Dogen's view, cooking is a chore before the real practice
for Dogen the cooking itself is the practice.
a Christian kitchen brother also said work and prayer were one time for him
Brother Lawrence, in a monastery kitchen, turning an omelet for the love of God.
Dogen and Brother Lawrence mean exactly the same thing
both bring full attention to the kitchen; Lawrence turns the work toward God, Dogen's cook to the rice itself.

games.q: your friend says chores just steal time from meditation. how might Dogen's cook answer?
o: if not now, when? the chore done with care is the practice.
true. hand chores off so there's more time to sit.
rush the chores so you can get back to the cushion.
games.why: the old cook wouldn't hand off the mushrooms: others are not me; if not now, when? the work itself was his practice.

practice: Do one small kitchen task now, or the closest thing within reach: rinse a cup, wipe a counter, fold a towel. Do it slowly, with both hands, as if the thing were your own eyes.
When the mind runs ahead to the next task, come back to the water and the cup.

wordCard.voice: Cooking as practice: rice, water and flame handled with full care, the work itself the practice, not a chore in its way.

carryVoice: In the kitchen: as your own eyes, the rice and the water. The mind at home, all nine, complete.
